opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the "human knockout" idea is one of the most exciting things to come out of these large biobanks. In a mouse lab, if you want to know what a gene does, you knock it out and watch what happens. We obviously can't do that in people. But nature has already run that experiment for us. Some people carry loss-of-function variants, so one or both copies of a gene simply don't work, and they've carried them since conception.

Mendelian randomization takes advantage of that. Your genotype is assigned more or less at random when you're conceived, before any lifestyle choices, environmental exposures, or diseases come along. So if we compare people who carry a variant that knocks down a gene, or lowers some biomarker, with people who don't, we get something close to a natural randomized trial. Confounding and reverse causation are much less of a problem than in a typical observational study.

What makes this practical now is scale. These variants are often rare, so you need hundreds of thousands of people with genotype data linked to health records, imaging, lab values, and outcomes over many years. Resources like the UK Biobank, and the population-scale sequencing efforts in Iceland, Finland, and other countries, give us enough carriers to ask real questions. For example, does lifelong reduced activity of this protein lower the risk of heart disease? Does it cause side effects anywhere else in the body?

That has big implications for drug development. The classic example is PCSK9. People with loss-of-function variants had low LDL cholesterol and fewer heart attacks, and they seemed otherwise healthy. That gave a lot of confidence that drugging that target would be both effective and safe. Today you can scan across thousands of traits, which is the phenome-wide approach, and see the full profile of what happens when a gene is turned down. That helps prioritize drug targets, flag likely adverse effects early, and sometimes find repurposing opportunities.

There are caveats we have to take seriously. A lifelong genetic knockout isn't the same as a drug you start at age sixty, because the body can compensate over development. Pleiotropy, where a variant affects several pathways, can violate the assumptions behind MR. And most of these biobanks are heavily skewed toward people of European ancestry, which limits both how far the findings generalize and how fair they are. Diversifying these cohorts is essential.

This is also where machine learning comes in for people like me. We can use it to better predict which variants are truly loss-of-function, extract richer phenotypes from imaging and clinical records, and handle the huge multiple-testing problem when you're testing every gene against every trait. Putting causal inference frameworks like MR together with modern ML on these datasets is a very promising way to move from correlation toward understanding what actually causes disease.

r001.rationale: The response says some people naturally carry loss-of-function variants that disable one or both gene copies, then explains that MR compares carriers with noncarriers to study reduced gene activity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that Mendelian randomization is really a way of borrowing the logic of a randomized trial from nature. At conception, you get a random shuffle of alleles from your parents, and that randomization is independent of all the lifestyle and environmental factors that normally confound observational studies. So if I find a variant that reliably changes the level or function of some protein, I can ask whether people carrying that variant have different rates of disease, and the answer tells me something causal about that protein rather than just correlational.

The "human knockout" angle is the extreme version of that. Traditionally, if you wanted to know what a gene does, you knocked it out in a mouse and watched what happened. Now, with biobanks on the scale of UK Biobank, Genes & Health, the Pakistani and Icelandic cohorts, and increasingly the All of Us program, you have hundreds of thousands to millions of people with sequencing data linked to decades of electronic health records. In that many people, you start finding individuals who carry loss-of-function variants in both copies of a gene. Nature has already done the knockout experiment for you, and the phenotype readout is a real human life rather than a mouse in a cage.

What makes that so powerful for drug development is that it's essentially a free phase two trial for a target. If people who are born without a functional copy of a gene are healthy and happen to have lower LDL, or lower triglycerides, or less risk of some disease, that's strong evidence that a drug inhibiting that protein would be both safe and effective. PCSK9 is the canonical story, where loss-of-function carriers had dramatically low cholesterol and no obvious harm, and that directly motivated the antibody therapies. ANGPTL3 and APOC3 followed a similar path. Conversely, if the knockouts show up with a serious adverse phenotype, you've learned that before spending a billion dollars.

There are caveats, of course. A lifelong genetic reduction isn't identical to a drug given in adulthood, there can be developmental compensation, and you have to be careful about pleiotropy and about population structure in the samples. Consanguineous populations are hugely valuable here because homozygous knockouts are far more common, but you have to make sure the health data is comparably rich. And the rare variants that give you the cleanest knockouts are, by definition, rare, so the statistical power often comes from aggregating across many cohorts and many loss-of-function alleles in the same gene.

But the broad picture, to me, is that we're moving from a world where human genetics was mostly used for discovery to one where it's a routine tool for causal inference and target validation. The biobanks give you the sample size, the sequencing gives you the knockouts, and Mendelian randomization gives you the framework to interpret them rigorously. That combination is probably the single most important shift in how we decide which biology to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response explains that inherited genetic variation can alter or eliminate a gene’s function, and that biobanks reveal people carrying natural loss-of-function variants, including knockouts in both gene copies.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting opportunity is to use naturally occurring genetic variation to understand what happens when a gene’s function is reduced or lost. With large human databanks, we can link those variants to health outcomes and look for people who effectively represent “human knockouts.”

Mendelian randomization gives us a framework for asking whether those genetically driven changes cause differences in disease risk. That could help us identify drug targets and anticipate potential side effects. But the assumptions matter: a variant may affect several biological pathways, and losing a gene’s function from birth isn’t necessarily equivalent to inhibiting it with a drug later in life. So it’s powerful evidence, but it needs careful interpretation and complementary validation.

r001.rationale: The response says naturally occurring genetic variation can reveal effects of reduced or lost gene function, and that databanks can identify people who effectively represent “human knockouts.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting opportunity is to use naturally occurring genetic variation to ask what happens when a particular gene’s function is reduced or lost. In a large human databank, you can identify people who carry those variants and connect that information to their health records and other measurements. That gives us a way to study something resembling a knockout in humans.

Mendelian randomization provides a framework for asking whether the resulting change in a biological pathway might actually cause a change in disease risk. Because genetic variants are inherited, they can help us get around some of the confounding that makes observational studies difficult. But it isn’t automatically a clean experiment: a variant may affect several pathways, and a lifelong genetic effect may differ from giving someone a drug later in life.

The scale is really important because these loss-of-function variants can be very rare. With enough people, we can start to understand both the potential benefits and the unintended consequences of disrupting a target, which could help us make better decisions about which therapies to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response explains that naturally occurring genetic variants can identify people with reduced or lost gene function, creating human knockouts, and describes Mendelian randomization as a framework for studying their effects.
